periods.activity_title: First Encounter — Poem Read-Aloud and Shared Reading

time_bands.activity: Activate prior knowledge by asking students what they know about Gilli Danda. Invite two or three students to mime swinging a danda or describe the game briefly.

Teacher reads the poem aloud expressively, emphasising the energetic rhythm and the rhyming pairs (around/sound, throw/go, free/see, flies/skies, fun/sun). Point to any classroom display or the textbook illustration as you name each image.

Shared reading: students follow in their textbooks (pp.79–80) while the teacher reads again. Pause after each stanza to ask one observation question — what do you notice about the playground? what do the children feel?
Choral reading of the whole poem once together. Encourage students to clap lightly on each rhyming word-ending to feel the poem's beat.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the poem's first full encounter; keep the pace lively so the rhythm is felt before comprehension work begins. Students who have played Gilli Danda will connect quickly to the playground imagery — let them share briefly before reading. Watch for unfamiliar words like 'underneath' and 'golden rays'; point them out without defining them fully yet.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think (p.80): answer questions on game, feelings, gilli's movement, outdoor lines.

time_bands.activity: Re-read the poem chorally once (from the choral reading of the full poem already done). This quick re-recite refreshes the text before discussion.

Let us Think — A. (p.80): discuss questions 1–3 as a class — which game is mentioned and what items are needed, how players feel, and what happens to the gilli when struck. Invite students to point to the relevant lines in their textbooks before answering.

Let us Think — A. (p.80): discuss questions 4–6 — which lines show outdoor play, the meaning of 'our game is so sound', and the word that shows happiness. Encourage students to justify answers with lines from the poem.
Whole-class consolidation: teacher summarises what the class has discovered about the poem's theme of outdoor joy and the spirit of never quitting.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the poem aloud and chorally, students come with the rhythm and imagery already in mind — build directly on those impressions. Question 5 ('our game is so sound') tends to puzzle students; guide them to infer 'sound' as 'strong and reliable' from context before offering the meaning. Unanchored questions 5 and 6 (word for happiness) may be assigned for written reflection in students' notebooks if time is short.

periods.activity_title: Guided Reading — Close Reading for Imagery and Inference

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think (p.80): re-examine outdoor imagery lines and the meaning of 'sound' through guided questions.

time_bands.activity: Brief warm-up: teacher reads the third stanza ('The small gilli, up high it flies…') aloud. Ask students to close their eyes and picture the scene described.
Guided reading in pairs: students re-read the poem stanza by stanza (pp.79–80), underlining one image they find most vivid in each stanza. Partners share their choices with each other.

Class discussion: collect the vivid images from each stanza — golden sun rays, bright blue skies, laughing together. Teacher guides students to see how the imagery builds a picture of outdoor freedom and community.
Students write two sentences in their notebooks explaining which image they liked best and why, drawing on the poem's own words as anchor phrases.

periods.teacher_notes: Having discussed the literal comprehension questions, this unit deepens engagement with the poem's imagery — the 'bright blue skies' and 'golden rays of the sun' are the central outdoor picture the poem paints. Students at Grade V can begin to talk about why a word or phrase works; encourage them to use the phrase itself in their explanation rather than only paraphrasing. The two-sentence written response also warms up the writing habit before the dedicated writing units.

periods.activity_title: Think and Discuss — Outdoor Play and Personal Experience

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think + Let us Speak + Let us Listen (p.80): discuss outdoor play enjoyment and name five favourite outdoor games.

time_bands.activity: Quick whole-class opener: teacher asks who has played a traditional outdoor game recently. One or two students share a sentence before the structured discussion begins.

Let us Think + Let us Speak + Let us Listen (p.80): guided discussion in pairs — Do you enjoy playing outdoors? Why or why not? Each student shares with a partner, then selected pairs share with the class.

Let us Think + Let us Speak + Let us Listen (p.80): in small groups, students name five outdoor games they enjoy. Each group nominates a speaker to share the group's list; teacher writes game names on the board to build a shared class list.

Whole-class reflection: teacher points to the poem's line 'with our friends, we never quit' and asks students to connect the poem's feeling to the outdoor games they just discussed. Two or three students respond aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked closely with the poem's imagery of communal outdoor play, students are well primed to connect the text to their own experience. Keep the group sharing brisk so every group gets a turn. The third discussion prompt (imagining yourself as the gilli) is not anchored in this unit — it can be offered as an optional spoken creative task for confident speakers or noted for the oracy unit that follows.

periods.activity_title: Let us Speak — Oral Presentation on a Group Game

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think + Let us Speak + Let us Listen (p.80): prepare and deliver a short oral presentation on a chosen group game.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models the presentation format using Gilli Danda as the example: name, indoor/outdoor, number of players, materials needed, key rules. Write the five points on the board as a scaffold.
Students work individually or in pairs for a quick unhurried preparation: they select a group game they know well and jot down the five points on a slip of paper or in their notebooks.
Presentations: five or six students (or pairs) take turns presenting their game to the class in under two minutes each. Class listens and may ask one question after each presentation.
Brief class discussion: which game described sounded the most fun and why? Teacher affirms the variety of traditional and contemporary games named.

periods.teacher_notes: Having discussed their favourite outdoor games together, students step naturally into a more structured presentation format here. The five-point scaffold (name, type, players, materials, rules) keeps presentations focused and models the kind of organised spoken English expected at Grade V. Students who are shy may present in pairs; ensure every student contributes at least one point aloud.

periods.activity_title: Let us Listen — Action Response to Poem Lines

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think + Let us Speak + Let us Listen (p.80): listen to poem lines and respond with matching actions.

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains the listen-and-respond activity: when a phrase from the poem is called out, students perform the matching action. Demonstrate all four actions slowly before beginning.

Unhurried practice round: teacher calls each phrase once at a steady pace — 'Swing and hit', 'Watch it go!', 'Laughing, playing', 'Shade your eyes from the sun' — students perform the action. Correct any mismatch between phrase and action together.
Full activity round: teacher calls the four phrases in varied order and at a quicker pace, repeating the sequence three to four times. Students listen carefully to the exact phrase before acting.
Pair variation: partners take turns calling the phrases for each other. Close with the whole class saying the poem's last stanza aloud while performing the actions together.

periods.teacher_notes: Having recited and discussed the poem extensively, students know its phrases well; this unit channels that familiarity into a physical, listening-focused response. The key skill is careful listening — students must wait for the exact phrase before acting, which trains attention. Watch for students who act on the first word heard rather than the complete phrase; use the slow demonstration round to address this.

periods.activity_title: Prefixes un- and re- — Meaning and Word Building

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn (p.81): add correct prefixes un- or re- to five base words and write each new word with its meaning.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the concept of prefixes using the poem's spirit: 'we never quit' — what if we said 'unwilling to quit'? Write 'un-' and 're-' on the board with their meanings (not, again). Use the textbook's example of 'unhappy' and 'redo' (p.81) to anchor the concept.

Let us Learn — A. (p.81): teacher works through 'write → rewrite' as a modelled example, writing the new word and meaning on the board. Students then work individually on the remaining four words: aware, comfortable, arrange, think.

Pairs compare their answers and discuss any word where both 'un-' and 're-' seem possible. Invite two or three pairs to share their choices with reasons; teacher addresses any disagreement (e.g. 'rethink' vs 'unthink' — both valid with different meanings).

Quick oral consolidation: teacher calls out four more everyday words (lock, load, tidy, fair) and students call back the prefixed form. Close by noting that prefixes are a tool for expanding vocabulary.

periods.teacher_notes: Students encountering 'uncomfortable' for the first time may confuse the base word boundary; show clearly that 'un-' attaches to 'comfortable', not 'comfort'. The word 'rethink' / 'unthink' distinction is worth a moment — rethink (think again) is common while unthink is unusual; accepting both with correct meanings is fair. Task B (abstract nouns grid) is not anchored here and may be noted as independent reading in students' textbooks.

periods.activity_title: Abstract Nouns — Sorting Concrete and Abstract Words

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn (p.82): sort the noun grid — encircle concrete nouns and identify abstract nouns including joy, anger, happiness, truth.

homework.task_brief: Let us Learn (p.82): think of three more abstract nouns not in the grid and write them in your notebook.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'joy' and 'leaf' on the board and asks: which can you hold in your hand? Establish the distinction — concrete nouns are things you can sense with your body; abstract nouns name feelings, ideas, qualities. Connect 'joy' to the poem's exuberant tone.

Let us Learn — B. (p.82): students work with the word grid in their textbooks. They encircle every noun they can see, taste, touch, or smell, and leave the feeling/idea words unencircled. Teacher circulates and prompts: 'Can you hold happiness? Can you taste truth?'

Whole-class check: teacher goes row by row through the grid, calling on students to say whether they encircled each word and why. Build the class list of abstract nouns on the board: joy, anger, truth, happiness, fear, lie.
Students suggest additional abstract nouns from their own vocabulary. Teacher accepts and writes a few on the board, confirming each with a quick 'can you see or touch it?' test.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked with prefixes that change meaning, students are already thinking about how words function — abstract noun sorting extends that vocabulary awareness. 'Lie' in the grid catches students off guard since it is also a verb; reassure them the grid treats it as a noun (an untruth) and in that sense it is abstract. The homework asks for three student-generated abstract nouns to extend the class list organically.

periods.activity_title: Possessive Pronouns — Completing Sentences with theirs, mine, yours, his, hers, ours

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn (p.83): fill blanks with the correct possessive pronoun from the given list for all six sentences.

time_bands.activity: Teacher sets up the concept with classroom objects: 'This pen belongs to me — it is mine. That book belongs to Arjun — it is his.' Write the six possessive pronouns (mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs) on the board and elicit one class-object example for each.
Let us Learn — C. (p.83): teacher reads sentence 1 aloud, models identifying who owns the crayons ('me') and selecting 'mine'. Students complete sentences 2–4 individually in their textbooks.
Students complete sentences 5–6, then compare answers with a partner. Class shares answers; teacher addresses any confusion between 'ours' (we) and 'theirs' (they) using a quick board contrast.
Oral consolidation game: teacher describes ownership of classroom items using 'belongs to' sentences and students call out the correct possessive pronoun. Move briskly through six to eight items.

periods.teacher_notes: Having sorted concrete and abstract nouns, students shift to a grammar-in-context task where ownership and identity are the key ideas. The most common error at this level is using 'their' (adjective) instead of 'theirs' (pronoun) — the distinction is that possessive pronouns stand alone without a following noun, and pointing to the textbook sentence pattern helps clarify this. The Jal Tarang context in sentence 4 is culturally rich; take a moment to acknowledge it if students are curious.

periods.activity_title: Dictionary Work and Sentence Writing — Key Poem Words

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write (p.85): look up meanings of quit, gather, swing, underneath, golden and write an original sentence for each.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models the process with the word 'playground' (not in the task but drawn from the poem): look it up in the dictionary, read the meaning aloud, then write one sentence using the word meaningfully — not just repeating the definition.

Let us Write — A. (p.85): students use their dictionaries to find meanings of 'quit' and 'gather', write the meaning briefly, then write one original sentence for each. Teacher circulates, checking that sentences use the word in context rather than restating its definition.
Students continue with 'swing', 'underneath', and 'golden', completing all five entries. Pairs briefly share their most interesting sentence with each other.
Two or three students read their favourite sentence aloud. Teacher highlights sentences that show clear understanding of meaning and encourages precise, vivid word use.

periods.teacher_notes: Having heard these words in the poem's energetic context, students approach the dictionary with some semantic expectation — guide them to check whether the dictionary meaning matches their sense before writing. Students often write definition-like sentences ('Golden means something that is gold coloured'); prompt them instead to place the word in a scene or action. Task B (question rearrangement) is not anchored here and is suitable for homework or independent work.

periods.activity_title: Question Formation — Rearranging Words to Form Questions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write (p.85): rearrange scrambled word groups to form correct questions with question marks — first four items.

homework.task_brief: Let us Write (p.85): rearrange the remaining four scrambled word groups (items 5–8) to form correct questions in your notebook.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes a scrambled set on the board ('you play do cricket') and thinks aloud while rearranging: identify the question word or helping verb, place it first, arrange subject and main verb, end with a question mark. Establish the rule: every question ends with '?'.

Let us Write — B. (p.85): students work individually to rearrange the first two scrambled groups ('are cows where the' and 'is your house which') in their notebooks. Teacher checks two or three students' work before the class shares answers.
Students tackle items 3 and 4 ('it time is what' and 'the blue why sky is'). Pairs compare and discuss any difference in word order. Class resolves disagreements together.
Teacher draws attention to question-word variety (where, which, what, why) used so far. Students read their four completed questions aloud with rising intonation.

periods.teacher_notes: Having written sentences using poem vocabulary, students now work on a structural feature of written English — correct question formation. The most frequent error is omitting the question mark or keeping statement word order; the modelled think-aloud at the start addresses both. Items 5–8 are sent home so writing practice continues beyond the sitting without overloading the in-class time.

periods.activity_title: Double Letters and Antonyms — Word-Level Writing Tasks

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write (p.85): write three words each for five double-letter patterns: tt, pp, ee, mm, bb.
Let us Write (p.87): circle the antonym of the underlined word for items 1–4.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reminds students of the double-'l' in 'gilli' and 'millet' (from the textbook's own example, p.85) and writes them on the board. Ask students to call out two more double-letter words they know to warm up the pattern-spotting skill.

Let us Write — C. (p.85): students independently write three words each for the double-letter patterns tt, pp, ee, mm, bb in their notebooks. Teacher circulates; prompt with rhyme families if students are stuck (e.g. for 'tt': butter, kitten, attend).
Let us Write — D. (p.87): teacher reads item 1 aloud ('expensive — precious / costly / cheap') and asks students to identify the odd one out by meaning. Students work through items 1–4 independently.

Class shares answers to Task D items 1–4; teacher clarifies any disagreement (e.g. why 'cheap' is the antonym of 'expensive' while 'precious' and 'costly' are synonyms). Items 5–8 of Task D are flagged as self-study.

periods.teacher_notes: The double-letter task builds on the poem's own vocabulary and sharpens spelling awareness; students who struggle may begin with patterns they already know (ee: tree, feet, meet) before attempting unfamiliar ones. Task D shifts to antonyms, which connects well to the earlier abstract noun and prefix work — a word's opposite meaning is itself a kind of prefix relationship (e.g. un- makes an antonym). Items 5–8 of Task D are left unanchored and suited to self-study.

periods.activity_title: Make a Gilli Danda — Craft with Waste Materials

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do + Just for Fun (pp.88–90): make a gilli and danda from waste material following the step-by-step instructions.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the instructions on pp.88–89 aloud, holding up the materials as each is named — thick twig (danda), short twig (gilli), rough stone for smoothening. Clarify safety: smooth surfaces carefully; no throwing indoors.

Students work in small groups to follow the steps: find the sticks (pre-collected and available on desks), smoothen the surfaces with the rough stone, shape the gilli ends, and optionally decorate with colour. Teacher circulates to assist and ensure safe handling.
Groups test their completed gilli and danda by setting the gilli on the floor and tapping it lightly — do not throw. Each group describes one thing they found challenging in making it.
Brief class reflection: how does making the game tool connect to the poem's celebration of Gilli Danda? Students share one-sentence responses.

periods.teacher_notes: All materials for this unit must be collected and placed on desks before the sitting begins — sticks, a smooth stone, and optional colours are needed for every group. Pre-cutting or pre-collecting is part of the teacher's preparation, not a student task from a prior sitting. The craft step requiring sharpening the gilli ends should be done by the teacher in advance if scissors or knives are not permitted; students then handle the already-shaped piece.
materials: Thick firm twigs (danda, one per group)
Short thick twigs 3–4 inches long (gilli, one per group)

periods.activity_title: Spellathon — Word-Making from the Letter Wheel

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do + Just for Fun (p.90): make as many three-or-more-letter words as possible from the letter wheel (A, C, E, T, H, E, R).

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws the seven letters A, C, E, T, H, E, R on the board in a wheel arrangement (referencing p.90). Explain the rule: letters can be used as many times as they appear in the wheel; a letter appearing once can only be used once per word. Demonstrate with 'Tea' and 'Reach'.

Individual silent work: students write as many three-or-more-letter words as they can find in four to five minutes. Then pairs pool their lists and look for words they each missed. Teacher circulates, prompting without giving words away.

Class list-building on the board: groups call out their words alphabetically; teacher writes each new one. Invite the class to try to find the seven-letter word using all the letters. (Answer: TEACHER)
Students create their own small letter wheel (four or five letters) in their notebooks. Partners try to find words in each other's wheel — a quick, playful close to the spellathon.

periods.teacher_notes: The spellathon builds spelling agility and vocabulary range in a playful format that sits naturally in the 'beyond the text' spirit. The seven-letter answer TEACHER is satisfying to discover as a class; hold it back until the last moment and let students feel the achievement. The personal wheel-making at the end gives every student a concrete creative product and doubles as an informal check of letter-sound awareness.

periods.activity_title: Riddle, Recitation and Celebration — Closing the Chapter

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do + Just for Fun (p.90): solve the 'your name' riddle and share solutions.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the riddle aloud from p.90 ('It belongs to you, but your friends use it more than you — what is it?') without giving the answer. Students think silently for a moment, then call out guesses. Arrive at the answer together: your name.

Recitation celebration: the whole class recites the poem 'Gilli Danda' together, this time with expressive actions — swinging, watching the gilli fly, clapping on the rhyme words. Let the recitation be joyful and energetic.
Students pair up and take turns reciting one stanza each for their partner, with the partner performing the matching actions. Partners give a thumbs-up for each rhyme word they hear correctly.

Brief whole-class share-out: students name one thing they learnt from the poem about outdoor play, friendship, or traditional games. Teacher closes by connecting the poem's 'we never quit' to the persistence they showed across the chapter's many tasks.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked through the poem's comprehension, language, craft, and puzzle work, students bring the full chapter to a close through joyful recitation and the riddle's gentle wit. The recitation here draws on everything built since the first read-aloud — rhythm, imagery, vocabulary, and the communal spirit the poem celebrates. Keep the closing share-out light and affirming; this is a moment of enjoyment, not evaluation.

items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 79 beginning "The small gilli, up high it flies". Which two things in the sky are mentioned in these lines to show that the children are playing outdoors?

options.label: B
options.text: Bright blue skies and golden rays of the sun

what_each_option_reveals.D: Students choosing this may be importing familiar sky imagery from other poems rather than reading the given lines carefully.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reveals a confusion between daytime outdoor imagery and nighttime sky descriptions.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Suggests the student associated 'flies' with other flying objects rather than tracking the poem's own descriptions.

items.item_stem: The poem says the children playing Gilli Danda 'never quit'. In two or three sentences, explain what feeling this phrase creates in the poem and how it connects to playing with friends.

expected_elements: Connects 'never quit' to determination or spirit.
Links the phrase to playing alongside friends.
Shows the phrase adds energy or motivation to the poem.

items.item_stem: Your teacher will call out one of the four phrases from the Gilli Danda poem — 'Swing and hit', 'Watch it go!', 'Laughing, playing', or 'Shade your eyes from the sun'. Listen carefully and perform the correct matching action. Which action goes with 'Watch it go!'?

options.text: For 'Watch it go!' you giggle or clap hands.
For 'Watch it go!' you keep your hands above your eyebrows to shade your eyes.
For 'Watch it go!' you pretend to swing an invisible danda.
For 'Watch it go!' you raise your arms as if you have just hit the gilli and are watching it fly.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statement 1 is true — raising the arms to watch the gilli fly is the correct action for 'Watch it go!'. Statements 2, 3, and 4 describe the actions for the other three phrases and are false for this phrase.

items.source_lo: Student makes a traditional game tool from waste materials, plays a letter-puzzle word game, and solves a riddle using a poem's cultural theme as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Craft-making of gilli and danda from twigs; spellathon with letters A, C, E, T, H, E, R; riddle about your own name.
items.item_stem: Using only the letters A, C, E, T, H, E, R (each letter used as many times as it appears), write three words of three or more letters. Then say aloud the seven-letter word that uses all the letters together.

expected_elements: Names three valid words of three-plus letters.
Each word uses only available letters correctly.
